extracted.intended_audience: NeurIPS 2026 reviewers and area chairs (peer reviewers for NeurIPS submissions)
extracted.subtask_description: Official NeurIPS 2026 guidance for reviewers and ACs on evaluating conference submissions, including general review criteria (Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality) and contribution-type-specific interpretations for General, Theory, Use-Inspired, Concept & Feasibility, and Negative Results papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution Type selection and immutability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should select the Contribution Type that best fits their submission. The review form is the same for all Contribution Types, but the way that reviewing criteria should be interpreted differ across Types. Reviewers should assess a submission according to the Contribution Type selected by the authors. It is not possible for Contribution Type to be changed after submission, either by the authors or by the reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contribution Types listed: General, Theory, Use-Inspired, Concept & Feasibility, Negative Results. Reviewers must interpret the general criteria in the light of the selected Contribution Type (e.g., empirical validation may be unnecessary for Theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: General — Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission technically sound? Are claims well supported (e.g., by theoretical analysis or experimental results)? Are the methods used appropriate? Is this a complete piece of work or work in progress? Are the authors careful and honest about evaluating both the strengths and weaknesses of their work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical correctness, appropriateness of methods, sufficiency of evidence for claims, and whether authors candidly discuss limitations. Quality spans from correctness to rigor of evaluation and honesty in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: General — Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written? Is it well organized? Does it adequately inform the reader? A superbly written paper provides enough information for an expert reader to reproduce its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity includes readability, organization, and inclusion of sufficient detail for reproduction by an expert. Poor organization or missing essential details are negative indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: General — Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results impactful for the community? Are others (researchers or practitioners) likely to use the ideas or build on them? Does the submission address a difficult task in a better way than previous work? Does it advance our understanding/knowledge on the topic in a demonstrable way? Does it provide unique data, unique conclusions about existing data, or a unique theoretical or experimental approach?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate real-world or community impact, novelty of insights, potential for reuse/adoption, improvement over prior work, and uniqueness of data or approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: General — Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work provide new insights, deepen understanding, or highlight important properties of existing methods? Is it clear how this work differs from previous contributions, with relevant citations provided? Does the work introduce novel tasks, problem framings, metrics, or methods that advance the field? Does this work offer a novel combination of existing techniques, and is the reasoning behind this combination well-articulated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality is not restricted to wholly new methods; novel insights from evaluating existing methods or demonstrating improved efficiency/fairness, or novel combinations with clear rationale, are valuable. Explicitly compare to prior work and cite relevant literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory — Quality (mathematical rigor and correctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical rigor and correctness. The primary criterion is the correctness of the claims. Proofs, lemmas, and the overall logical flow must be mathematically sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should examine core arguments sufficiently to establish high confidence, even if not verifying every line. Correctness is paramount for theoretical contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory — Appropriateness of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriateness of assumptions. Theoretical results may require assumptions, but the standard for 'good' assumptions varies by the type of contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh assumptions against novelty of the result and norms in existing literature; unrealistic or unstated assumptions reduce value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory — Empirical validation is not necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical validation is not necessary. Theoretical contributions may stand on their own and the purpose of designing new algorithms in this context need not be to outperform state-of-the-art applied models or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theory paper shouldn’t be penalized for lacking experiments. If empirical results are included, they can be used to further study formalized insights rather than to compete with state-of-the-art applied models or large benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory — Clarity (intuition alongside rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity requires both readability of the artifact and whether authors should outline the high-level proof strategy or the intuition behind a new mathematical definition before diving into technical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide high-level intuition and proof sketches so readers can follow the motivation and structure of arguments before technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory — Clear scoping of contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must clearly signpost its type of theoretical contribution early on and the distinction between novel contributions and prior work must be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state what is new vs. what is existing work; early signposting helps reviewers and readers understand the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory — Significance (types of impactful theoretical contributions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance should be evaluated based on the specific type of theoretical contribution the paper aims to make. Reviewers may look for impact in one or more of the following areas: Novel Abstractions and Formulations; Progress on Established Problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of significance: new theoretically rigorous frameworks/definitions giving new vocabulary; progress on community problems; surfacing new angles or solving open problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory — Originality (technical novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality can take several forms depending on the paper's goal. It might be a fundamentally new proof technique, a novel synthesis of tools from other disciplines (e.g., statistical physics, pure mathematics), or a completely new way to parameterize or define a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical novelty in methods, proof techniques, cross-disciplinary synthesis, and new problem formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-Inspired — Quality (real and meaningful use case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the use case real and meaningful? A use case should not be artificially constructed to present an interesting methodological problem. Rather, it should arise from the pre-existing needs of users outside the NeurIPS community, and this motivation should be made clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the use case is motivated by real external needs and not contrived for methodological novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-Inspired — Design matched to the use case
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the design matched to the use case? Use-inspired submissions should closely tie their task framing, methods, metrics, etc. to the needs of a use case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods may need to accommodate data structure, physical constraints, or be evaluated with metrics such as interpretability or robustness; evaluate whether design choices align with these needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-Inspired — Expectation of non-standard datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect 'non-standard' datasets. Submissions in this Contribution Type will frequently be evaluated on real-world datasets that fall outside common ML benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such datasets should be encouraged if justified in relation to the use case; reviewers should not penalize non-benchmark datasets if they are appropriate and well-justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-Inspired — Clarity (for an ML audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity should be measured in relation to an ML audience. While the use case in question may provide motivation for the submission, the authors should not require the reader to have expertise in the domain of application and should explain any relevant jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must make domain-specific jargon accessible to ML readers and ensure the work is understandable without domain expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-Inspired — Significance (use-case and community impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance can encompass both the potential for impact on an important use case and impact for the broader NeurIPS community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel ideas that are simple to apply in practice may be especially valuable. Prior work outside ML should be considered; compare novel methods vs. commonly used non-ML approaches as well as baseline ML methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-Inspired — Originality (formulation or combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality need not mean wholly novel methods. It could mean a novel combination of existing methods to match the characteristics of the data, or a novel way of framing a stereotypical ML problem due to the particular needs of the use case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers should provide insights to guide methods development; when applying existing methods in a new context, discuss why certain choices are effective or ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept & Feasibility — Quality (strongly supported claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strongly supported claims. As with papers in the general category, the submission must be technically sound and claims must be rigorously grounded through some combination of empirical, analytical, and conceptual arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope of ideas may exceed what can be validated in a single paper, but claims must still be strongly supported. This contrasts with workshop submissions where ideas may be only partially supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept & Feasibility — Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written? Is it well organized? Does it adequately inform the reader? A superbly written paper provides enough information for an expert reader to reproduce its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same reproducibility and organization expectations as general submissions; clarity helps signal broader feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept & Feasibility — Significance (high potential to change approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: High potential for changing our approaches and/or understanding. The significance bar for Concept and Feasibility papers is high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The promise of the paper should go significantly beyond the specific evaluations included; evaluations should be chosen to indicate broader significance and potential to change paradigms or practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept & Feasibility — Originality (high novelty bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly novel ideas. The originality bar for Concept and Feasibility papers is high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty of ideas and whether they plausibly change how important classes of problems may be approached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Results — Quality (grounded analysis and experimentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounded analysis and experimentation. In addition to the quality standards for a general paper, it is important that the negative result not be simply an empirical observation that some experiment did not turn out as expected or hoped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative results should be grounded in deeper analysis via conceptually-informed conjectures, careful experimentation, rigorous proofs, or combinations thereof; superficial failures are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Results — Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written? Is it well organized? Does it adequately inform the reader? A superbly written paper provides enough information for an expert reader to reproduce its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same clarity/reproducibility expectations as general submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Results — Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes our understanding of an important question. The significance bar for Negative Results papers is high. The negative result should be informative in changing how the community addresses a question or exposing that the community should be addressing an important question in a different way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A negative result relating to something few people would need or want is not significant. A Negative Results paper need not identify a path to mitigate the negative finding; that can be left to future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Results — Originality (unexpected/surprising)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected or surprising in some way. The originality bar for Negative Results papers is high. The negative result must be surprising or unexpected in some way — that is, it should run counter to a popularly held understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial or obvious negative results (e.g., 'a linear classifier cannot separate a nonlinear decision boundary') are not original even if correct; novelty requires surprising insight.
